 1   I.      INTRODUCTION

 2            The old way of litigating privacy class actions hasn’t been working. Far too often, it’s

 3   resulted in anemic settlements that primarily benefit the lawyers—settlements focused on credit

 4   monitoring, cy pres, or that were just hastily reached. See, e.g., Frank v. Gaos, 139 S. Ct. 1041,

 5   1047–48 (2019) (Thomas, J., dissenting); In re Tiktok Consumer Priv. Litig., No. 20-cv-04699,

 6   dkt. 316 (N.D. Ill. Jan. 25, 2024) (“It is not unusual for a case of such significance to be

 7   vigorously litigated for years; yet here the Original Plaintiffs reached a settlement in principle

 8   only nine days after the JPML issued its consolidation order.”). It’s an open secret in the

 9   defense bar that most settlements are driven by the lowest deal the Court will accept, with

10   plaintiffs’ lawyers abdicating real opposition.1 That gives the Court a Hobson’s choice when

11   given a settlement: reject it and restart litigation, or try to make improvements on the edges.

12            There’s a better way, but it starts with doing the work the Court is doing now:

13   appointing class counsel that will steer the case away from that path. But that process is tough.

14   To start, the rules of decision are fuzzy: the reality is that the express Rule 23(g) factors are met

15   by most experienced firms. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g) (e.g., experience, knowledge of the law).

16   The bulk of the actual decision-making, then, gets made under the nebulous mandate of “any

17   other matter” pertinent to counsel’s abilities. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g)(1)(B).

18           That’s challenging enough, but it gets harder still. The Court is told that it must act as a

19   “fiduciary” for the class, but the class is a party appearing before it—putting the Court in the

20   uncomfortable position of, for a moment, doing things like weighing in on the best strategy to

21   pursue in a case that the Court presides over. Because of the dissonance of that dual role, the

22   Court’s usual function—resolving a sharply disputed question between opposing parties—

23   suddenly seems like choosing sides. When it comes to picking class counsel, courts

24   understandably prefer agreed slates of leadership over a subjective, ambiguous inquiry.

 1          But one analogy for approaching this problem, as we’ve argued before, is that the Court

 2   is acting as an “in-house counsel” picking an outside firm for a client of millions. And that

 3   analogy makes clear why a competition—like the one the Court is holding—is a good thing:

 4   for instance, no in-house counsel would hire an “agreed” slate of firms who showed up at one’s

 5   door (surely, with promises that there’d be no duplicative billing), or counsel without a

 6   meaningful strategy. Instead, in-house counsel would ask what the firms’ track records were in

 7   similar cases, what the costs would be, what specific theories they would advance, their views

 8   about the actual value of the case, and how they would realize that value.

 9          How, then, can a Court take an objective approach to deciding what’s in the best

10   interests of its temporary, millions-strong client? A burgeoning area of scholarship suggests a

11   surprising but commonsense solution: perhaps we should just ask them. See Alissa del Riego &

12   Joseph Avery, The Class Action Megaphone: Empowering Class Members with an Empirical

13   Voice, 76 Stan. L. Rev. Online 1 (2023); Alissa del Riego & Joseph Avery, Inadequate

14   Adequacy?: Empirical Studies on Class Member Preferences of Class Counsel, 2024 Utah L.

15   Rev. 499 (2024). And that’s just what we did.

19   counsel to adopt and what characteristics the lead firm should have. The Professors were able

20   to reach nearly 400 independent, putative Class Members. And the results were clear:

27          •       Characteristics of the firm. The most important factor to the Class was

28   significant experience in privacy class actions, closely followed by experience with state

 1   II.     BACKGROUND

 2            After 23andMe announced a data breach in October 2023, a deluge of class action

 3   complaints followed—to date, a total of 39 in federal court, now consolidated before this

 4   Court.2 Relying on its own in-house forensics team, Edelson researched and developed the

 5   allegations in the Melvin Plaintiffs’ complaint that uniquely explains the unprecedented harms

 6   facing the Class and the particularly vulnerable subset of individuals—Jewish and Chinese

 7   people, so far—whose data was marketed on the Dark Web with the all-but-explicit invitation

 8   that these individuals be targeted for (as Representative Gottheimer put it) “domestic

 9   extremism.” (Melvin v. 23andMe, Inc., 24-cv-00487-EMC, dkt. 1, ¶¶ 36, 39, 42, 47, 49, 53

10   (N.D. Cal.) (herein, “Melvin.”)) The Melvin Plaintiffs’ complaint (also uniquely) seeks

11   forward-looking relief that responds to that harm in the form of threat assessment and

12   monitoring. (Id. ¶¶ 119–30.) Finally, while many complaints re-reported the method of attack

13   as “credential stuffing,” the Melvin Plaintiffs were the only plaintiffs to explain exactly why

14   that mode of attack makes the liability case especially strong here: 23andMe should have been

15   able to detect the breach and respond to it months before the company announced the breach

16   occurred. (Id. ¶¶ 69–83.) Since the complaint’s filing, 23andMe has been forced to admit that

17   was right: the breach began in April 2023, which 23andMe was able to detect on review.3

26          C.      Our Joint Research on Class Counsel and Class Member Preferences
27          26.     Our joint research has focused on developing and exploring ways to provide class
28   members with a much-needed seat and voice in class action litigation, especially through the use

      EXPERT REPORT OF JOSEPH J. AVERY, PH.D.,
      J.D., AND ALISSA DEL RIEGO, J.D.                -4-                     CASE NO. 24-MD-03098-EMC
      Case 3:24-cv-00487-EMC Document 41-1 Filed 04/18/24 Page 8 of 62



 1   of surveys, technology, and behavioral science tools that enable a better understanding of class
 2   members’ preferences.
 3          27.     Our research outlines the many representational problems in class action litigation,
 4   focusing on the lack of communication between class counsel and the class members they
 5   represent. See Alissa del Riego & Joseph J. Avery, The Class Action Megaphone: Empowering
 6   Class Members with an Empirical Voice, 76 Stan. L. Rev. Online 1, 1–4 (2023) (“Class Action
 7   Megaphone”).
 8          28.     These representational problems begin at the outset of the litigation, as class
 9   members presently provide no input on which attorneys the court, pursuant to Rule 23(g),
10   appoints as interim class counsel to represent class members in the litigation. See id.; Alissa del
11   Riego & Joseph Avery, Inadequate Adequacy?: Empirical Studies on Class Member Preferences
12   of Class Counsel, 2024 Utah L. Rev. 499 (2024) (“Inadequate Adequacy”). Even after class
13   counsel is chosen, absent class members are afforded no opportunity to weigh in on the claims
14   asserted, injuries pled, remedies sought, and the litigation strategies employed to secure those
15   remedies. As a result, the ensuing litigation and any class-wide settlements often sacrifice
16   remedies favored by the class in exchange for others favored by class counsel (i.e. remedies that
17   would result in greater compensation to the attorneys at the class’s expense). See Class Action
18   Megaphone, at 3-4.
19          29.     Indeed, class members are only entitled to communicate their preferences as
20   objectors to settlements. However, practically speaking, class members lack sufficient knowledge
21   to make reasoned and well-informed objections because of the communication void that exists
22   between them and class counsel throughout the litigation. Id. Courts naturally defer to class
23   counsel’s nearly irrefutable claims that it obtained the best outcome possible, given the
24   undisclosed, confidential information uncovered in discovery and the uncertainties and delays
25   that accompany further litigation and a potential trial and appeal. Id.
26          30.     While there are obvious impracticalities associated with involving thousands or
27   millions of class members in litigation decisions, our research demonstrates these realities should
28   not preclude class members from having any voice in the litigation. Id. at 4.

 1          31.     Starting with the appointment of interim class counsel, courts use the Rule 23(g)
 2   factors as a guide to appoint the attorneys “best able to represent the interests of the class.” Fed.
 3   R. Civ. Proc. 23(g)(2). Our research shows, however, that courts may not necessarily choose the
 4   same attorneys that the class would choose for themselves. While courts undoubtedly have unique
 5   expertise in applying 23(g), these decisions can be assisted by knowing what class members
 6   actually prefer in their attorneys based on the context of any given case. We dive into this in our
 7   article published this Spring in the Utah Law Review titled Inadequate Adequacy?: Empirical
 8   Studies on Class Member Preferences of Class Counsel. See generally Inadequate Adequacy,
 9   2024 Utah L. Rev. 499 (2024).
10          32.     In the article, we surveyed individuals about the type of counsel they would want
11   in three real class actions in which multiple attorneys applied to serve as class counsel: a products
12   liability class action, a data breach class action, and a data privacy class action. Id. at 522–25. We
13   provided class members with a summary of the claims raised against each of the defendants in the
14   litigation and a brief biography or description of the attorneys that applied to represent the class
15   based on those attorneys’ own submissions to the district court when they applied to serve as
16   interim class counsel in the particular case. Id. We asked survey respondents generally about their
17   preferences in counsel and then specifically as to which attorneys they would choose. Id.
18          33.     We note two key findings from this research:
19          34.     First, surveyed participants valued Rule 23(g)’s appointment criteria (experience,
20   knowledge of the law, resources willing to dedicate to the litigation, and work done identifying
21   and investigating claims) but also valued other factors such as attorneys’ integrity,
22   trustworthiness, and willingness to listen to class members. Id. at 526–33.
23          35.     Second, surveyed participants invariably chose different attorneys and/or attorney
24   teams than those ultimately appointed by the court, despite indicating that they value the same
25   Rule 23(g) criteria courts applied. Id. at 535–40.
26          36.     These findings indicate that there can be a disconnect between what courts think
27   class members want and what they actually want. Our proposed solution to this problem is
28   “representational notice.” Id. at 543–51. Representational notice involves notice to and a survey

      EXPERT REPORT OF JOSEPH J. AVERY, PH.D.,
      J.D., AND ALISSA DEL RIEGO, J.D.                 -6-                     CASE NO. 24-MD-03098-EMC
      Case 3:24-cv-00487-EMC Document 41-1 Filed 04/18/24 Page 10 of 62



 1   of a sample of identifiable class members at the outset of class litigation and prior to the
 2   appointment of class counsel. Id. at 543–46. The notice is meant to inform class members of their
 3   potential claims and to learn about their preferences. Id. at 543–49. Practically, it affords a subset
 4   of class members an opportunity to convey their preferences on counsel, claims, litigation
 5   strategies, and litigation outcomes to the court and prospective class counsel. Id. at 547–49.
 6          37.      Representational notice is not meant to supplant the court’s ultimate obligation to
 7   appoint class counsel and interim class counsel under Rule 23(g). Courts have unique expertise
 8   and responsibilities that cannot and should not be replaced with class members’ preferences. But
 9   courts, pursuant to Rule 23(g)(1)(B) that permits them to consider any “matter pertinent to
10   counsel’s ability to fairly and adequate represent the interests of the class,” should consider and
11   acknowledge class members’ preferences when appointing counsel. Id. at 550–51.
12          38.      Obtaining and openly discussing class member preferences via representational
13   notice has multiple benefits, not least the following:
14          39.      Legitimacy and transparency. The process of selecting class counsel becomes
15   more open when prospective class members have the opportunity to respond to representational
16   notice, even if the court eventually appoints different attorneys. If the court’s selection aligns with
17   the preferences of the sampled class members, it enhances the perceived legitimacy of the
18   appointment. Conversely, if the court appoints counsel contrary to the members’ preferences,
19   transparency is achieved when the court provides an explanation for its decision, thereby
20   acknowledging the difference and justifying its choice of representation.
21          40.      Affording class members a voice. The essence of class litigation is to serve the
22   interests of the entire class, yet, traditionally, class members have lacked any means to engage or
23   express their preferences, with the exception of a select few representatives chosen by the
24   attorneys. This is a rather serious deficiency, and it is one that scholars, such as us, are
25   increasingly working to redress. Providing class members with the means to voice their opinions
26   offers valuable insights to both prospective class counsel and the court regarding their choice of
27   representation, the harms they seek to address, and their desired outcomes in the litigation.
28   Although class counsel must balance the collective best interests with practical considerations,

 1   incorporating the perspectives of class members should guide their approach in advancing the
 2   lawsuit.
 3             41.     Avoiding bias. Without insight into class members’ preferences, courts are forced
 4   to act in a vacuum, relying on their own preferences and deciding under the influence of their
 5   own biases. While this is not necessarily a negative—after all, such decisions fall within courts’
 6   purview for good reason—additional information regarding class members’ preferences would
 7   undoubtedly be useful and would provide alternative and perhaps countervailing perspectives. In
 8   other words, while both courts and class members will bring their own biases to evaluating
 9   counsel, the combined effect should be a more complete evaluation of attorneys, better
10   understanding of the class and its preferences, and a more balanced selection outcome. Id. at 543.
11             42.     Based on our research, we recommend that courts employ representational notice
12   or similar mechanisms to solicit class preferences on counsel, litigation strategy, and litigation
13   outcomes prior to appointing interim class counsel in consolidated actions. That is what the
14   survey described below was designed to do, and it can assist the Court in appointing lead counsel
15   in this matter.

     5       The Bonferroni correction is a method used in statistical analysis to reduce the likelihood
24   of obtaining false-positive results when multiple hypothesis tests are conducted simultaneously.
     To understand it in practical terms, consider a legal scenario where multiple pieces of evidence
25   are being presented. Each piece of evidence is scrutinized to determine if it significantly supports
     the case. The more pieces of evidence there are, the higher the chance that at least one will appear
26   to be significant purely by chance, even if it’s not truly related to the case at hand. Applying the
     Bonferroni correction is akin to raising the standard of proof for each individual piece of evidence
27   when the overall quantity of evidence is large. It tightens the criteria that each piece of evidence
     must meet to be considered statistically significant. By doing so, it controls for the risk of a false
28   positive, ensuring that the evidence deemed significant is more likely to be genuinely pertinent to
     the case and not just a result of chance due to the high number of tests.

26   target a demographically relevant subset of a potential class exceeding 7 million individuals, the
27   finite nature of our sample precludes a complete encapsulation of the diverse perspectives within
28   the entire class. While our sample size was statistically powered to yield significant insights, the

 5   handle the case without being constrained by its own finances)?” (Ex. 1-C, at 12.) The results
 6   were a mean of 6.29 with standard deviation of .96. Both the p-value and the adjusted p-value
 7   were less than .001. Second, class members wanted a firm that would temper its own financial
 8   aspirations: “How important is it to you that the law firm representing the class agrees to seek
 9   attorneys’ fees of no more than 20% of the settlement fund?” The mean approached 6.0 and was
10   highly significant. (Ex. 2, Data Sheet, at 7.)
11          92.     Now that we have discussed the questions with quantitative outcomes, it is worth
12   discussing the single open-ended survey question, wherein respondents were given space to opine
13   about whatever factors or issues they deemed important and/or relevant. While analysis of
14   qualitative responses poses challenges, there are a few strands we picked up. First, and
15   dovetailing with the just-discussed quantitative results, respondents emphasized that firms should
16   communicate with them. This included transparency in the process, such as keeping class
17   members apprised of updates and answering questions that might arise (e.g., one respondent
18   wondered if a deceased family member who otherwise qualified did, indeed, qualify). This also
19   included a general desire to be heard, to have class members’ opinions be taken into
20   consideration. After all, the incentives for counsel do not perfectly align with those of class
21   members, especially when class members seek non-pecuniary outcomes.
22          93.     In addition, of the various Rule 23(g) factors, in their open-ended responses,
23   respondents emphasized experience and knowledge. This accords with the quantitative outcomes
24   discussed above.
25   VI.    CONCLUSION
26          94.     Our comprehensive analysis has illuminated the critical factors that class members
27   are looking for in their legal representation for this specific class action against 23andMe.

Based on your answers to the questions, you may be a class member in a class action lawsuit

What’s a class action?: A class action is a lawsuit in which an individual or individuals called
“class representatives” bring a single lawsuit on behalf of themselves and other people (“class
members”) who have similar legal claims.

What is this case about?: In 2023, the private genetic information of approximately 7 million
23andMe customers was breached by hackers. The breached information included customers’
genetic heritage, ancestral origin, full names, home addresses, profile pictures, and birth dates.
Hackers have already posted some of this information on hidden internet marketplaces,
specifically targeting members of certain vulnerable groups.

23andMe is facing several lawsuits for:

   1.   Negligence in not protecting customer data adequately,
   2.   Not informing customers promptly about the breach,
   3.   Violating consumer protection laws, and/or
   4.   Violating state genetic privacy laws.

based on applications submitted by the law firms. The legal team chosen will make crucial

        Strategy 1: Some attorneys believe that the best way to help the class is to negotiate the
        case privately with 23andMe and settle the case quickly by using a third-party mediator,
        directly obtaining information from 23andMe on a voluntary basis, and resolving the case
        before the court weighs in on the validity of the claims.

        The pros of this strategy include lower risk (i.e., greater certainty in the case’s outcome
        and greater certainty in securing some compensation for the class), and a speedy
        resolution. The cons of this strategy are that it can result in smaller settlements or
        incomplete relief due to the lack of full information about the extent of the defendant’s
        actions, the data breach, and the breach’s negative effects.

        Strategy 2: Some attorneys believe that the best way to help the class is to work through
        the public court system before reaching a settlement. The goal is to obtain full
        information through the formal court-supported discovery process and to get a sense of
        the strength of the class’s claims by first advancing them in court.

        The pros of this strategy include the possibility of a larger settlement or more complete
        relief resulting from a fuller picture of the defendant’s conduct, the extent of the data
        breach, and the breach’s negative effects on class members. The cons of this strategy are
        that it could be riskier (i.e., less certainty in the case’s outcome and less certainty of

Q1. The law firms seeking to represent the class disagree about which litigation strategy to pursue:
Strategy 1 : Some attorneys believe that the best way to help the class is to negotiate the case privately with 23andMe and
settle the case quickly by using a third-party mediator, directly obtaining information from 23andMe on a voluntary
basis, and resolving the case before the court weighs in on the validity of the claims.
The pros of this strategy include lower risk (i.e., greater certainty in the case’s outcome and greater certainty in securing
some compensation for the class), and a speedy resolution. The cons of this strategy are that it can result in smaller
settlements or incomplete relief due to the lack of full information about the extent of the defendant’s actions, the data
breach, and the breach’s negative effects.

Strategy 2 : Some attorneys believe that the best way to help the class is to work through the public court system before
reaching a settlement. The goal is to obtain full information through the formal court-supported discovery process and to
get a sense of the strength of the class’s claims by first advancing them in court.
The pros of this strategy include the possibility of a larger settlement or more complete relief resulting from a fuller
picture of the defendant’s conduct, the extent of the data breach, and the breach’s negative effects on class members. The
cons of this strategy are that it could be riskier (i.e., less certainty in the case’s outcome and less certainty of obtaining
compensation for class members) and that it takes longer to resolve the case.

CAND 435
(Rev. 08/2018)                                                                         INSTRUCTIONS
Use this form to order the transcription of a record of proceedings. CJA counsel should use Form CJA24. Before completing this form, please visit cand.uscourts.gov/transcripts
for complete transcript ordering information. THESE INSTRUCTIONS SUPPLEMENT THE WEBSITE INFORMATION.
      1.     Complete a separate order form for each case number for which transcripts are ordered.
      2.     Complete a separate order form for each court reporter who reported proceedings in the case.
      3.     Complete Items 1-12. Keep a copy of your completed order form for your records.
      4.     E-file this form in the U.S. District Court CM/ECF system. Exceptions to e-filing: (a) sealed cases/proceedings; (b) non-parties; (c) pro se parties who are not e-filers.
             In such cases, mail or hand-deliver a hard copy addressed to the court reporter supervisor (email list available at cand.uscourts.gov/transcripts/contact) at the
             Court division where the proceeding was held.
      5.     Next, the court reporter/transcriber will contact you to confirm estimated costs and delivery options. Deliver payment to the court reporter/transcriber promptly.
             Upon receipt of the deposit, the court reporter/transcriber will begin work on the transcript.
      6.     Unless prepayment is waived, delivery time is computed from the date the court reporter/transcriber receives the deposit, authorized CJA 24 Form, authorization
             from Federal Public Defender’s Office or, for transcripts ordered by the U.S. government, from the date of receipt of the DCN number.
      7.     The deposit fee is an estimate. Any overage will be refunded; any shortage will be due from you.
                                                                          ITEM-BY-ITEM INSTRUCTIONS (ITEMS 1-12):
Items 1-3        In fields 1a, 2a & 3a, please provide the contact name and information for the person responsible for ordering the transcript. In a law office, this is usually a
                 paralegal or administrative assistant, not the attorney. In fields 1b, 2b & 3b, provide the attorney name and contact info, if the attorney is not the contact person.
Items 5-6.       Only one case number may be listed per order.
Item 7.          Visit cand.uscourts.gov/transcripts for instructions for determining the name of the court reporter who reported the proceeding or if the proceeding was audio-
                 recorded. If minutes have not been filed, contact the court reporter supervisor at the division where the hearing was held.
Item 8.          Check appeal OR non-appeal AND criminal OR civil. In forma pauperis: a court order specifically authorizing transcripts is required before transcripts may be
                 ordered in forma pauperis.
Item 9a.         List specific date(s) of the proceedings for which transcript is requested. A transcript of only a portion of a proceeding may be ordered, if the description is clearly
                 written to facilitate processing. Under “type,” indicate briefly what type of proceeding it was, such as “motion,” “sentencing,” or “CMC.”
Item 9b.         Select desired FORMAT(S) for transcript. There is an additional charge for each format ordered. Visit cand.uscourts.gov/transcripts/rates for details. Unlock
                 ECF/web access is included at no extra charge with each of the other formats.
Item 9c.         There are 7 DELIVERY TYPES to choose from (times are computed from date of receipt of the deposit fee or DCN number). NOTE: Full price may be charged only if
                 the transcript is delivered within the required time frame. For example, if an order for expedited transcript is not completed and delivered within 7 calendar days,
                 the 14-day delivery rate would be charged.
                   TRANSCRIPT DELIVERY TIMES:
                    ORDINARY ─ 30 calendar days.
                    14-DAY ─ 14 calendar days.
                    EXPEDITED ─ 7 calendar days.
                    3-DAY ─ 3 calendar days
                    DAILY (NEXT DAY) ─ Following adjournment and prior to the normal opening hour of the court on the following morning whether or not it actually is a court day.
                    HOURLY (SAME DAY) ─ within two (2) hours.
                    REALTIME ─ A draft unedited, uncertified transcript produced by a certified realtime reporter as a byproduct of realtime to be delivered electronically during
                         proceedings or immediately following adjournment.
Item 11.         Sign in this space to certify that you will pay all charges (the deposit plus any additional charges.) An electronic or conformed (/s/) signature is acceptable.
Item 12.         Enter the date of signing the order and certification.

Motion to Stay Proceeding Pending Transfer by the Judicial Panel on MDL [dkt 37] -Held.
          Case 3:23-cv-05147-EMC Document 78 Filed 02/26/24 Page 2 of 3




                                           SUMMARY
       23andMe’s motion for a stay pending a decision by the JPML is granted. This ruling,
however, does not preclude a plaintiff from moving for relief from the stay should, e.g., an
urgent matter arise.

      The Court rejects the Melvin plaintiffs’ suggestion that a stay should be denied because of
23andMe’s alleged sale of genetic information. They have failed to show that there is a nexus
between that conduct and the alleged misconduct at issue in the pending suits as framed by the
complaints (i.e., the data breach).

       The Court also rejects any suggestion that the Court should engage in the process of
appointment of interim counsel before the JPML makes its decision. The JPML hearing is set
for March 28, 2024. Engaging in the process of appointment of interim counsel now makes little
sense when the JPML hearing is just a month (approximately) away and there are a number of
cases with counsel who are not formally before this Court.

        The Court emphasized that all parties should be expected to proceed expeditiously once
the JPML does render its decision and if the consolidation is ordered and assigned to this Court
(e.g., moving forward with appointment of interim counsel, the filing of a consolidated amended
complaint, etc.). In order to expedite matters should this Court retain jurisdiction over multiple
class actions), the Court agrees with the plaintiffs that it would be helpful to set in advance
guidelines on motions for appointment of interim counsel.

                   •   A motion to appoint may (but need not) propose a slate of counsel from
                       different firms. Whether counsel come from the same firm or from
                       different firms, the Court encourages a team of diverse attorneys (e.g.,
                       years of experience, backgrounds). It would be helpful for motions to
                       appoint to address, inter alia, what work has been done in this case
                       specifically and on other data breach or comparable cases, and resources
                       available.
                   •   The motion should explain how work will be allocated among counsel,
                       how duplication of efforts will be minimized, and cost efficiencies
                       maintained.
                   •   The motion should set forth a proposed case plan.
                   •   Any motion to appoint shall be filed within one week after the JPML
                       issues decision. Each motion shall be no longer than 12 pages in length.
                   •   Any response to a motion to appoint shall be filed one week
                       thereafter. Each response shall be no longer than 6 pages in length and
                       shall address any and all motions in a single responsive brief.
                   •   So long as the JPML promptly issues its decision following the March 28
                       hearing, if the matter is assigned to this Court, the Court expects to have a
                       hearing on the motions to appoint in late April or early May together with
                       an initial CMC.
          Case 3:23-cv-05147-EMC Document 78 Filed 02/26/24 Page 3 of 3




        Finally, the Court notes that its ruling here is predicated on its understanding (as
affirmed by 23andMe) that 23andMe has put in place litigation holds and taken the necessary
preservation steps to ensure that relevant evidence is not destroyed, whether or not inadvertently.

 1          Pursuant to Northern District Local Rule 7-11 and this Court’s December 1, 2022 Standing Order,

 2   Defendant 23andMe, Inc. (“23andMe”) respectfully requests leave to file a reply Plaintiffs’ Response to

 3   Defendant’s Motion for Extension.

 4          On February 12, 2024, 23andMe filed its Administrative Motion to Continue Deadline to Respond

 5   to the Complaint Until After Case Management Conference, ECF No. 23 (the “Motion”). Plaintiffs filed a

 6   Response to the Motion on February 16, 2024, ECF No. 26 (the “Response”). In the Response, Plaintiffs

 7   assert numerous misstatements and misrepresentations of the record, including but not limited to: (1) that

 8   they oppose 23andMe’s extension request based on a news article issued this week—which is not true, as

 9   Plaintiffs have never agreed to an extension since February 1, 2024, when 23andMe first requested it; (2)

10   that 23andMe is launching unprecedented research projects—which is not true, as 23andMe has provided

11   its customers the option to consent to medical research that may be relevant to them for years; (3) that a

12   continuance of 23andMe’s response deadline is not warranted until 23andMe provides assurances of its

13   security practices—which is irrelevant, because the Incident did not arise from 23andMe’s security

14   practices, which have been for years above industry standard for direct-to-consumer genetic companies,

15   but arose from a credential stuffing attack on a narrow subset of accounts that used login credentials

16   compromised from other platforms; and (4) that 23andMe agreed to stipulate to waive its right to compel

17   arbitration—which is not an accurate statement of record of the parties’ correspondence.

18          23andMe seeks leave file a reply that corrects this misstatements and mischaracterizations of the

19   record, and 23andMe’s reply will aid the Court in its ruling on 23andMe’s Motion. See In re Cathode Ray

20   Tube (CRT) Antitrust Litig., No. 3:14-CV-02510, 2014 WL 7206620, at *1 n.2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 18, 2014)

21   (granting leave to file a surreply “in the interests of completeness and judicial efficiency.”)

22          For the reasons stated, 23andMe respectfully requests leave to file a four-page Reply to the

23   Response.

 1          Plaintiffs Melvin and J.L.’s (the “Melvin Plaintiffs”) Opposition to 23andMe’s motion for a

 2   continuance—the only opposition filed to a request for a continuance in any of the Related Cases—is

 3   riddled with falsities in an attempt to tell the Court there is a fire when there is no smoke.

 4          Melvin and J.L.’s suit is the second-to-last of the Related Cases 1 filed at the end of January 2024,

 5   immediately after their counsel backed out of their earlier agreement to participate in mediation of the

 6   Related Cases, which was attended in person or by proxy by plaintiffs firms involved in every single other

 7   action subject to 23andMe’s pending MDL application. The Melvin Plaintiffs have provided no valid or

 8   true reason for expediting their near-last filed claims, apart from their counsel’s very public desire to be

 9   appointed as leader of a putative class—a motion that was filed concurrently with the Melvin Plaintiffs’

10   complaint and which this Court has already summarily denied. ECF No. 15.

11          Instead, the Melvin Plaintiffs paint a false narrative under the auspice of requiring some kind of

12   immediate relief in their Opposition to 23andMe’s motion for continuance (“Opposition”) (ECF No. 26).

13          First, the Melvin Plaintiffs claim they are opposing 23andMe’s Motion based on an allegedly new

14   discovery this week regarding 23andMe allowing its users to participate in research. Not so. In fact, the

15   Melvin Plaintiffs have refused to grant 23andMe any extension whatsoever from the time their counsel

16   first reached out on February 1, 2024. See Declaration of Rebekah Guyon In Support of Defendant’s

17   Administrative Motion to Continue Deadline to Respond to Complaint, at ¶ 6 (ECF No. 23-1). The only

18   thing that changed in the past fifteen days is that on the evening of Valentine’s Day, the Melvin Plaintiffs’

19   lawyers came up with a pretext for their refusal to grant the same extension entered to date by stipulation

20   or court order in these Related Cases (except, as noted below, the grounds cited are based on false and

21   unfounded accusations). Supplemental Declaration of Rebekah Guyon In Support of 23andMe’s

22   [Proposed] Reply In Support of the Motion (“Supp. Guyon Decl.”), ¶ 2.

23          Second, 23andMe has not announced, nor have the Melvin Plaintiffs discovered, any new practices.

24   As 23andMe responded to the Melvin Plaintiffs’ counsel on February 15, 2024, 23andMe has publicly

25   disclosed that it has provided its customers with the opportunity to participate in third-party medical
